arXiv:1708.07412v1 [math.AG] 23 Aug 2017

The Milnor number of plane branches with tame semigroups of values

A. Hefez, J.H.O. Rodrigues and R. Salomão

Universidade Federal Fluminense - Niterói
Abstract.

The Milnor number of an isolated hypersurface singularity, defined as the codimension μ⁡(f)\mu(f) of the ideal generated by the partial derivatives of a power series ff that represents locally the hypersurface, is an important topological invariant of the singularity over the complex numbers. However it may loose its significance when the base field is arbitrary. It turns out that if the ground field is of positive characteristic, this number depends upon the equation ff representing the hypersurface, hence it is not an invariant of the hypersurface. For a plane branch represented by an irreducible convergent power series ff in two indeterminates over the complex numbers, it was shown by Milnor that μ⁡(f)\mu(f) always coincides with the conductor c⁡(f)c(f) of the semigroup of values S⁡(f)S(f) of the branch. This is not true anymore if the characteristic of the ground field is positive. In this paper we show that, over algebraically closed fields of arbitrary characteristic, this is true, provided that the semigroup S⁡(f)S(f) is tame, that is, the characteristic of the field does not divide any of its minimal generators.

Keywords: Singularities in positive characteristic, Milnor number in positive characteristic, Singularities of algebroid curves

2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 14B05, 14H20, 14D06, 32S05

1. Introduction

Several aspects of the local study of singularities of algebraic varieties may be reduced to the study of algebroid varieties. In particular, by a singular algebroid plane curve we mean a scheme C=Spec⁡(𝒪)C=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal{O}), where (𝒪,𝔪)(\mathcal{O},{\mathfrak{m}}) is a local one-dimensional complete kk-algebra, with kk any algebraically closed field, such that dim𝔪/𝔪2=2\dim{\mathfrak{m}}/{\mathfrak{m}}^{2}=2. From the completeness of 𝒪\mathcal{O}, for any choice of generators x,yx,y of the ideal 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}}, there is a surjection φ:k⁡[[X,Y]]→𝒪\varphi\colon k[[X,Y]]\to\mathcal{O}, where k⁡[[X,Y]]k[[X,Y]] is the ring of formal power series in two indeterminates with coefficients in kk. The kernel of this surjection is a principal ideal ⟨f⟩\langle f\rangle, which generator ff is uniquely determined up to a multiplication by a unit in k⁡[[X,Y]]k[[X,Y]], which we call an equation of CC. If we define 𝒪f=k⁡[[X,Y]]/⟨f⟩\mathcal{O}_{f}=k[[X,Y]]/\langle f\rangle, and write Cf=Spec⁡(𝒪f)C_{f}=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_{f}), we have that 𝒪≃𝒪f\mathcal{O}\simeq\mathcal{O}_{f} and CfC_{f} is isomorphic to CC as a scheme over kk. When CC is an integral scheme, we call it a plane branch.

Two algebroid curves C1=Spec⁡(𝒪1)C_{1}=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_{1}) and C2=Spec⁡(𝒪2)C_{2}=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_{2}) will be considered equivalent, writing C1∼C2C_{1}\sim C_{2}, when they are isomorphic as kk-schemes, that is, when 𝒪1≃𝒪2\mathcal{O}_{1}\simeq\mathcal{O}_{2} as kk-algebras. In this case, if f1f_{1} is an equation of C1C_{1} and f2f_{2} is an equation of C2C_{2}, then f1f_{1} and f2f_{2} are related by the existence of an automorphism Φ\Phi and a unit uu of k⁡[[X,Y]]k[[X,Y]] such that f2=u⁡(f1∘Φ)f_{2}=u(f_{1}\circ\Phi). In this situation, we say that f1f_{1} and f2f_{2} are contact equivalent.

Given f∈k⁡[[X,Y]]f\in k[[X,Y]], the ideal T⁡(f)=⟨f,fX,fY⟩T(f)=\langle f,f_{X},f_{Y}\rangle is called the Tjurina ideal of ff and the dimension τ⁡(f)\tau(f) of the kk-vector space k⁡[[X,Y]]/T⁡(f)k[[X,Y]]/T(f) is the so called Tjurina number of ff. It is easy to check that this number is invariant under contact equivalence, so it defines an invariant of CC, denoted by τ⁡(C)\tau(C) or τ⁡(𝒪)\tau(\mathcal{O}).

The ideal J⁡(f)=⟨fX,fY⟩J(f)=\langle f_{X},f_{Y}\rangle is called the Jacobian ideal of ff and plays an important role when k=ℂk=\mathbb{C}. The Milnor number μ⁡(f)\mu(f) of ff is the dimension as kk-vector space of k⁡[[X,Y]]/J⁡(f)k[[X,Y]]/J(f). From the chain rule it is immediate to verify that μ⁡(f)=μ⁡(Φ⁡(f))\mu(f)=\mu(\Phi(f)) for any automorphism Φ\Phi of k⁡[[X,Y]]k[[X,Y]].

When f∈ℂ​{X,Y}f\in\mathbb{C}\{X,Y\}, the ring of convergent complex power series, Milnor proves by topological methods that μ⁡(u​f)=μ⁡(f)\mu(uf)=\mu(f) for any unit uu in ℂ​{X,Y}\mathbb{C}\{X,Y\}. In arbitrary characteristic this does not hold as one can see from the very simple example below.

Example 1.1.

Let char⁡k=p\operatorname{char}\,{k}=p and f=Yp+Xp+1∈k⁡[[X,Y]]f=Y^{p}+X^{p+1}\in k[[X,Y]]. Then CfC_{f} is a plane branch such that τ⁡(Cf)=p2\tau(C_{f})=p^{2} and

μ⁡(f)=∞,whileμ⁡((1+Y)​f)=p2≠μ⁡(f).\mu(f)=\infty,\ \ \quad{\rm while}\ \ \quad\mu((1+Y)f)=p^{2}\neq\mu(f).

From the inclusion J⁡(f)⊂T⁡(f)J(f)\subset T(f), it is clear that τ⁡(f)⩽μ⁡(f)\tau(f)\leqslant\mu(f). So, one always has μ⁡(f)<∞⇒τ⁡(f)<∞\mu(f)<\infty\ \Rightarrow\tau(f)<\infty. In characteristic zero, one also has the converse of the above implication. In positive characteristic, this converse may fail, as one can see from Example 1.1 above.

Since the ideal that defines the singular locus of a curve C=CfC=C_{f} is its Tjurina ideal T⁡(f)T(f), it is natural to say that a curve CC has an isolated singularity if 0<τ⁡(C)<∞0<\tau(C)<\infty.

Notice that this is a well posed definition, since τ⁡(f)=τ⁡(g)\tau(f)=\tau(g) when ff and gg are contact equivalent. So, in characteristic zero, to say that CfC_{f} has an isolated singularity is equivalent to say that 0<μ⁡(f)<∞0<\mu(f)<\infty, but not in arbitrary characteristic.

There is an easy criterion in arbitrary characteristic (cf. [B, Proposition 1.2.11]) for a plane curve CfC_{f} to have an isolated singularity:

CfC_{f} has an isolated singularity if and only if ff is reduced.

In contrast, the fact that ff is reduced is not sufficient to guarantee that μ⁡(f)<∞\mu(f)<\infty as shows Example 1.1. Also, the vanishing of one of the partial derivatives of ff implies μ⁡(f)=∞\mu(f)=\infty, but this is not a necessary condition, as the following example shows.

Example 1.2.

Let char⁡k=3\operatorname{char}\,{k}=3 and f=X2​Y+Y2​X∈k⁡[[X,Y]]f=X^{2}Y+Y^{2}X\in k[[X,Y]]. We have that f=X​Y​(X+Y)f=XY(X+Y) is reduced, but fXf_{X} and fYf_{Y} are both nonzero and have the common factor Y−XY-X, implying that μ⁡(f)=∞\mu(f)=\infty.

The preceding examples highlight the need of a better notion of Milnor number and this was treated in our previous work [HRS, Section 3] in the more general context of hypersurfaces. There we were led to define the Milnor number of C=CfC=C_{f} as μ⁡(C)=e0​(T⁡(f))\mu(C)=e_{0}(T(f)), where e0​(−)e_{0}(-) stands for the Hilbert-Samuel multiplicity of an ideal. This number is invariant in the contact class of ff. Also, a criterion was given there to recognize if an isolated hypersurface singularity CC satisfies μ⁡(C)=μ⁡(f)\mu(C)=\mu(f) for any of its equations ff. Namely it is shown in [HRS, Theorem 4.8] that this holds if and only if fℓ∈ℳ​T​(f)ℓf^{\ell}\in\mathcal{M}T(f)^{\ell} for some positive integer ℓ\ell, where ℳ\mathcal{M} is the maximal ideal of k⁡[[X1,…,Xn]]k[[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]].

Our aim in the present work is to study plane branches over arbitrary algebraically closed fields. In characteristic zero, the Milnor number μ⁡(f)\mu(f) coincides with the conductor c⁡(f)c(f) of the semigroup of values S⁡(f)S(f) of the branch 𝒪f\mathcal{O}_{f} (cf. [Mi]), where the semigroup of values of 𝒪\mathcal{O} is the set of all finite intersection multiplicities of ff with plane algebroid curves and c⁡(f)c(f) is the smallest integer α∈S⁡(f)\alpha\in S(f) such that α+ℕ⊂S⁡(f)\alpha+\mathbb{N}\subset S(f). Since these notions are invariant in the contact class of ff, then we may define S⁡(C)=S⁡(f)S(C)=S(f) and c⁡(C)=c⁡(f)c(C)=c(f) and have that

C1∼C2⇒S⁡(C1)=S⁡(C2)andc⁡(C1)=c⁡(C2).C_{1}\sim C_{2}\ \Rightarrow\ S(C_{1})=S(C_{2})\quad\text{and}\quad c(C_{1})=c(C_{2}).

In arbitrary characteristic, Deligne proved in [De] (see also [MH-W]) the inequality μ⁡(f)⩾c⁡(Cf)\mu(f)\geqslant c(C_{f}) and shows that the difference μ⁡(f)−c⁡(Cf)\mu(f)-c(C_{f}) is the number of wild vanishing cycles associated to ff.

Our main result is the proof that Milnor’s number μ⁡(f)\mu(f) of ff and the conductor c⁡(Cf)c(C_{f}) of a branch CfC_{f} coincide when the characteristic does not divide any of the minimal generators of the semigroup of values S⁡(Cf)S(C_{f}). If this is so, we call S⁡(Cf)S(C_{f}) a tame semigroup. Our proof was inspired by a result of P. Jaworski in the work [Ja2], which we simplified and extended to arbitrary characteristic, under the appropriate assumptions. We would like to point out that in the process of writing our results, E. García-Barroso and A. Ploski published the paper [GB-P], where they show, by other methods, a weaker version of our main result (with the converse), in the particular case when pp is greater than the multiplicity mult⁡(f){\rm mult}(f) of ff. They also observed that (contrary to ours) their proof fails when p≤mult⁡(f)p\leq{\rm mult}(f). The proof we give of the result, without the restriction p>mult⁡(f)p>{\rm mult}(f), is more subtle.

We should also mention that H.D. Nguyen in [Ng] has shown, in the case of several branches, a generalization of this equality, but also under a strong restriction on the characteristic. In the irreducible case, the restriction is p>c⁡(Cf)+mult⁡(f)−1p>c(C_{f})+{\rm mult}(f)-1.

This work is part of the PhD Thesis of the second author, under the supervision of the other two authors.

2. A fundamental formula

Let 𝒪\mathcal{O} be the ring of a singular plane branch CC with maximal ideal 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}}. Consider the integral closure 𝒪¯{\overline{\mathcal{O}}} of 𝒪\mathcal{O} in its field of fractions. The ideal 𝒞⁡(𝒪)=(𝒪:𝒪¯)\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{O})=(\mathcal{O}:{\overline{\mathcal{O}}}) is called the conductor ideal of 𝒪¯{\overline{\mathcal{O}}} in 𝒪\mathcal{O}. This is the largest common ideal of 𝒪\mathcal{O} and 𝒪¯{\overline{\mathcal{O}}}. As an ideal of 𝒪¯≃k⁡[[t]]{\overline{\mathcal{O}}}\simeq k[[t]] we have tc​𝒪¯=𝒞⁡(𝒪)t^{c}{\overline{\mathcal{O}}}=\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{O})\, for some c∈ℕc\in\mathbb{N}. This number cc coincides with the conductor c⁡(C)c(C) of the semigroup of values S⁡(C)S(C).

Choose generators x,yx,y of 𝔪\mathfrak{m} and a uniformizing parameter t∈𝒪¯t\in{\overline{\mathcal{O}}} such that the images x⁡(t)x(t) and y⁡(t)y(t) in 𝒪¯≃k⁡[[t]]{\overline{\mathcal{O}}}\simeq k[[t]] are a primitive parametrization for any equation ff of CC determined by the kernel of the epimorphism k⁡[[X,Y]]→𝒪k[[X,Y]]\rightarrow\mathcal{O} given by X↦xX\mapsto x and Y↦yY\mapsto y, that is k⁡((x⁡(t),y⁡(t)))=k⁡((t))k((x(t),y(t)))=k((t)). We say that z∈𝔪z\in{\mathfrak{m}} is a transversal parameter for 𝒪\mathcal{O} if v⁡(z)=min⁡{v⁡(w)|w∈𝔪}v(z)=\operatorname{min}\{v(w)\,|w\in{\mathfrak{m}}\} where v=ordtv=\mathop{\rm ord}\nolimits_{t} is the natural valuation of 𝒪¯{\overline{\mathcal{O}}}, which coincides with the intersection index with ff, in the sense that v⁡(g)=I⁡(f,G)v(g)=\operatorname{I}(f,G), where G∈k⁡[[X,Y]]G\in k[[X,Y]] is any representative of the residual class g∈𝒪g\in\mathcal{O}. This minimum is called the multiplicity of CC and is denoted mult⁡(C){\rm mult}(C). We also say that zz is a separable parameter with respect to tt if z′​(t)=d​zd​t≠0z^{\prime}(t)=\frac{dz}{dt}\neq 0. For h∈k⁡[[X,Y]]h\in k[[X,Y]], we will write fxf_{x} for fX​(x,y)∈𝒪f_{X}(x,y)\in\mathcal{O} and similarly for fyf_{y}.

The following fundamental formula is classical and is attributed to D. Gorenstein. In order to have a proof in arbitrary characteristic, for the convenience of the reader, we will reproduce the one found in [Ga, Appendix, page 101], as communicated to us by K. O. Stöhr.

Theorem 2.1.

([Go, Theorem 12]) Let 𝒪\mathcal{O} be the ring of an algebroid plane branch CC. If x,yx,\,y is any system of generators of 𝔪⊂𝒪{\mathfrak{m}}\subset\mathcal{O} and ff is an equation of CC corresponding to the embedding determined by xx and yy, then

v⁡(fy)=c⁡(f)+v⁡(x′).v(f_{y})=c(f)+v(x^{\prime}).

Proof: The proof will be by induction on the number of blowing-ups necessary to dessingularize the branch CC. If 𝒪\mathcal{O} is already non-singular then the result is obvious.

We treat first the case in which xx is both a transversal and separable parameter and the tangent line is YY. Since in this coordinate system the tangent cone of an equation ff is YnY^{n}, where n=mult⁡(C)n={\rm mult}(C), then, if f(1)f^{(1)} is the strict transform of ff, we have Xn​f(1)​(X,Z)=f⁡(X,Y)X^{n}f^{(1)}(X,Z)=f(X,Y) where Y=X​ZY=XZ. Differentiation with respect to ZZ in the last relation leads to

Xn​fZ(1)​(X,Z)=X​fY​(X,Y).X^{n}f_{Z}^{(1)}(X,Z)=Xf_{Y}(X,Y).

This relation modulo ⟨f⟩\langle f\rangle, after cancelling XX, gives xn−1​fz(1)=fy.x^{n-1}f_{z}^{(1)}=f_{y}. Hence

v⁡(fy)=v⁡(xn−1)+v⁡(fz(1))=n⁡(n−1)+v⁡(fz(1)).v(f_{y})=v(x^{n-1})+v(f_{z}^{(1)})=n(n-1)+v(f_{z}^{(1)}).

By the induction hypothesis v⁡(fz(1))=v⁡(x′)+c⁡(f(1))v(f_{z}^{(1)})=v(x^{\prime})+c(f^{(1)}). According to a well known formula (see for instance [He, Formula 6.10]), we have that c⁡(f)=c⁡(f(1))+n⁡(n−1)c(f)=c(f^{(1)})+n(n-1), which gives us the result in this case.

Suppose now that x,yx,\,y is an arbitrary set of generators of 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}}. It is clear that there exists a system of generators z,wz,\,w of 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}} such that

x=a​z+b​w,y=c​z+d​wx=az+bw,\ \ \ \ y=cz+dw

where a,b,c,d∈ka,b,c,d\in k with D=a​d−b​c≠0D=ad-bc\neq 0 and, say, zz is both a transversal and separable parameter of 𝒪\mathcal{O} and WW is the tangent line. Then, for any equation g∈k⁡[[X,Y]]g\in k[[X,Y]] corresponding to the embedding determined by zz and ww, we get gw=fx​b+fy​d.g_{w}=f_{x}b+f_{y}d. It follows that

fy​D​z′=(d​x′−b​y′)​fy=d​x′​fy+b​x′​fx=x′​gw,f_{y}Dz^{\prime}=(dx^{\prime}-by^{\prime})f_{y}=dx^{\prime}f_{y}+bx^{\prime}f_{x}=x^{\prime}g_{w},

therefore, v⁡(x′)+v⁡(gw)=v⁡(z′)+v⁡(fy)v(x^{\prime})+v(g_{w})=v(z^{\prime})+v(f_{y}).

Since by the preceding case we have v⁡(gw)=c⁡(g)+v⁡(z′)v(g_{w})=c(g)+v(z^{\prime}) and since c⁡(g)=c⁡(f)c(g)=c(f), this leads to v⁡(fy)=c⁡(f)+v⁡(x′)v(f_{y})=c(f)+v(x^{\prime}) in this general case.  

We will need another formulation for Theorem 2.1, which is quoted in the literature as Delgado’s Formula (cf. [Ca, Proposition 7.4.1]), proved over ℂ\mathbb{C}, which extends naturally to arbitrary algebraically closed fields.

To begin with, let 𝒪\mathcal{O} be the ring of an algebroid plane branch CC and choose an equation ff for CC. For g∈𝒪fg\in\mathcal{O}_{f}, take a representative G∈k⁡[[X,Y]]G\in k[[X,Y]] of gg and define

[f,g]:=fx​Gy¯−fy​Gx¯∈𝒪andg′​(t):=dd​t​G​(x⁡(t),y⁡(t)).[f,g]\colon=f_{x}\overline{G_{y}}-f_{y}\overline{G_{x}}\in\mathcal{O}\,\quad\mbox{and}\,\quad g^{\prime}(t)\colon=\frac{d\,}{dt}G(x(t),y(t)).

Notice that [f,g][f,g] and g′​(t)g^{\prime}(t) are well defined since they do not depend on the representative GG of gg. With these notations we have

Corollary 2.2.

Let 𝒪\mathcal{O} be the local ring of a plane algebroid branch CC. Fix a uniformizing parameter tt for 𝒪\mathcal{O} and let ff be an equation for CC. Then, for every g∈𝒪g\in\mathcal{O}, one has

v⁡([f,g])=c⁡(f)+v⁡(g′​(t)).v([f,g])=c(f)+v(g^{\prime}(t)).

Proof: Let (x⁡(t),y⁡(t))(x(t),y(t)) be a local parametrization of CC. From f⁡(x⁡(t),y⁡(t))=0f(x(t),y(t))=0 we obtain fX​(x⁡(t),y⁡(t))​x′+fY​(x⁡(t),y⁡(t))​y′=0f_{X}(x(t),y(t))x^{\prime}+f_{Y}(x(t),y(t))y^{\prime}=0, hence it is easy to check that

x′​(fY​GX−fX​GY)​(x⁡(t),y⁡(t))=fY​(x⁡(t),y⁡(t))​(g′​(x⁡(t),y⁡(t))).x^{\prime}(f_{Y}G_{X}-f_{X}G_{Y})(x(t),y(t))=f_{Y}(x(t),y(t))(g^{\prime}(x(t),y(t))).

We deduce the result computing the orders in the preceding equality and using Theorem 2.1.  

Remark 2.3.

Since v⁡(fx)=c⁡(f)+v⁡(y′)⩾cv(f_{x})=c(f)+v(y^{\prime})\geqslant c and v⁡(fy)=c⁡(f)+v⁡(x′)⩾cv(f_{y})=c(f)+v(x^{\prime})\geqslant c, we conclude that

j=⟨fx,fy⟩⊂𝒞⁡(𝒪).\mathrm{j}=\langle f_{x},f_{y}\rangle\subset\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{O}).

Since 𝒪\mathcal{O} is Gorenstein, this implies that

τ⁡(𝒪)=dimk𝒪/j⩾dimk𝒪/𝒞⁡(𝒪)=dimk𝒪¯/𝒪=c2.\tau(\mathcal{O})=\dim_{k}\mathcal{O}/j\geqslant\dim_{k}\mathcal{O}/\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{O})=\dim_{k}\overline{\mathcal{O}}/\mathcal{O}=\frac{c}{2}.

If p=char⁡kp=\operatorname{char}{k} and f∈k⁡[[X,Y]]f\in k[[X,Y]] is irreducible, then

v⁡([f,g])⩾c⁡(f)+v⁡(g)−1,v([f,g])\geqslant c(f)+v(g)-1,

with equality holding if and only if p∤v⁡(g)p\nmid v(g).

Proof: This follows from the previous Corollary and from v⁡(g)−1⩽v⁡(g′​(t))v(g)-1\leqslant v\Big(g^{\prime}(t)\Big) where equality holds if and only if p∤v⁡(g)p\nmid v(g).  

3. Milnor number for plane branches

For the definitions and notation used in this section we refer to [He] where these notions are characteristic free. Let f∈ℳ⊂k⁡[[X,Y]]f\in\mathcal{M}\subset k[[X,Y]] be an irreducible power series, where kk is an algebraically closed field of characteristic p⩾0p\geqslant 0 and ℳ=⟨X,Y⟩\mathcal{M}=\langle X,Y\rangle. Let us denote by S⁡(f)=⟨v0,…,vg⟩S(f)=\langle v_{0},\ldots,v_{g}\rangle the semigroup of values of the branch CfC_{f}, represented by its minimal set of generators, where the number gg is called the genus of S⁡(f)S(f). These semigroups have many special properties that will be used throughout this section and which we describe briefly below.

Let us define e0=v0e_{0}=v_{0} and denote by ei=gcd⁡{v0,…,vi}e_{i}=\gcd\{v_{0},\ldots,v_{i}\} and by ni=ei−1/ein_{i}=e_{i-1}/e_{i}, when i=1,…,gi=1,\ldots,g. The semigroup S⁡(f)S(f) is strongly increasing, which means that vi+1>ni​viv_{i+1}>n_{i}v_{i}, for i=0,…,g−1i=0,\ldots,g-1, (cf. [He, 6.5]). This implies that the the sequence v0,…,vgv_{0},\ldots,v_{g} is nice, which means that ni​vi∈⟨v0,…,vi−1⟩n_{i}v_{i}\in\langle v_{0},\ldots,v_{i-1}\rangle, for i=1,…,gi=1,\ldots,g (cf. [He, Proposition 7.9]). This, in turn, implies that the semigroup S⁡(f)S(f) has a conductor c⁡(f)c(f), which is given by the formula (cf. [He, 7.1])

c⁡(f)=∑i=1g(ni−1)​vi−v0+1.c(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{g}(n_{i}-1)v_{i}-v_{0}+1.

The semigroup S⁡(f)S(f) is also symmetric (cf. [He, Proposition 7.7]), that is,

∀z∈ℕ,z∈S⁡(f)⟺c⁡(f)−1−z∉S⁡(f).\forall\,z\in\mathbb{N},\ z\in S(f)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ c(f)-1-z\not\in S(f).

Moreover, any element x∈S⁡(f)x\in S(f) may be written in a unique way as x=∑i=0gxi​vix=\sum_{i=0}^{g}x_{i}v_{i} with x0∈ℕx_{0}\in{\mathbb{N}} and 0⩽xi⩽ni−10\leqslant x_{i}\leqslant n_{i}-1. We refer to this representation as the canonical representation of xx.

Recall that we defined a semigroup of values of a plane branch to be tame if p=char⁡(k)p=\operatorname{char}(k) does not divide any element in its minimal set of generators.

A first property of curves with tame semigroups is the following:

Lemma 3.1.

If C=Spec⁡(𝒪)C=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal{O}) is a branch with tame semigroup S⁡(C)S(C), then, for any equation ff of CC, one has that μ⁡(f)<∞\mu(f)<\infty.

Proof: Let ff be an equation for CC. We have that μ⁡(f)=∞\mu(f)=\infty if and only if there is an irreducible q∈k⁡[[X,Y]]q\in k[[X,Y]] that divides both fXf_{X} and fYf_{Y}, say fX=A​qf_{X}=Aq and fY=B​qf_{Y}=Bq, for some A,B∈k⁡[[X,Y]]A,\,B\in k[[X,Y]]. If this is so, we write the canonical representation of the intersection multiplicity I⁡(f,q)∈S⁡(f)∖{0}\operatorname{I}(f,q)\in S(f)\setminus\{0\} as ∑i=ℓgxi​vi\sum_{i=\ell}^{g}\,x_{i}v_{i}, xi∈ℕx_{i}\in\mathbb{N}, where ℓ∈{0,…,g}\ell\in\{0,\ldots,g\} is the least index ii for which xi>0x_{i}>0 and we take h∈k⁡[[X,Y]]h\in k[[X,Y]] such that I⁡(f,h)=vℓ\operatorname{I}(f,h)=v_{\ell}. Then [f,h]=q⁡(A​hY−B​hX)[f,h]=q\left(Ah_{Y}-Bh_{X}\right), and hence by computing intersection multiplicities with ff, and using that S⁡(f)S(f) is tame, we get that

vℓ+c⁡(f)−1=∑i=ℓgxi​vi+γ,with​γ∈S⁡(f).v_{\ell}+c(f)-1=\sum_{i=\ell}^{g}\,x_{i}v_{i}\,+\gamma,\,\,\mbox{with}\,\,\gamma\in S(f).

Since xℓ>0x_{\ell}>0, this gives the absurd equality (the summation is taken to be zero if ℓ=g\ell=g)

Recall that two plane analytic branches over the complex numbers are equisingular if their semigroups of values coincide. We will keep this terminology even in the case of positive characteristic.

The following example will show that μ⁡(Cf)=e0​(T⁡(f))\mu(C_{f})=e_{0}(T(f)) may not be constant in an equisingularity class of plane branches.

Example 3.2.

The curves given by f=Y3−X11f=Y^{3}-X^{11} and h=Y3−X11+X8​Yh=Y^{3}-X^{11}+X^{8}Y are equisingular with semigroup of values S=⟨3,11⟩S=\langle 3,11\rangle. In characteristic 33, one has that μ⁡(Cf)=μ⁡((1+Y)​f)=30\mu(C_{f})=\mu((1+Y)f)=30 and μ⁡(Ch)=μ⁡((1+X)​h)=24\mu(C_{h})=\mu((1+X)h)=24. Notice that in this case SS is not tame.

The following is an example which shows that the μ\mu-stability is not a character of an equisingularity class.

Example 3.3.

Let S=⟨4,6,25⟩S=\langle 4,6,25\rangle be a strongly increasing semigroup with conductor c=28c=28. Consider the equisingularity class determined by SS over a field of characteristic p=5p=5. If f=(Y2−X3)2−Y​X11f=(Y^{2}-X^{3})^{2}-YX^{11}, which belongs to this equisinsingularity class, we have that μ⁡(f)=41\mu(f)=41 and μ⁡(Cf)=30\mu(C_{f})=30, hence CfC_{f} is not μ\mu-stable. But from [HRS, Theorem 4.8], the equisingular curve with equation h=(Y2−X3+X2​Y)2−Y​X11h=(Y^{2}-X^{3}+X^{2}Y)^{2}-YX^{11} is μ\mu-stable, since h3∈ℳ​T​(h)3h^{3}\in\mathcal{M}T(h)^{3}. In this case one has μ⁡(h)=μ⁡(Ch)=29\mu(h)=\mu(C_{h})=29. Notice that here, again, SS is not tame.

We now state our main result, which proof will occupy the rest of the paper.

Theorem 3.4 (Main Theorem).

If C=Spec⁡(𝒪)C=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal{O}) is a plane singular branch with S⁡(C)S(C) tame, then μ⁡(f)=μ⁡(C)=c⁡(f)\mu(f)=\mu(C)=c(f) for any equation ff of CC. In particular, CC is μ\mu-stable.

The proof we give of this theorem is based on the following theorem which was stated without a proof over the complex numbers in [Ja1], but proved in the unpublished work [Ja2]. Our proof, in arbitrary characteristic, is inspired by that work, which we suitably modified in order to make it work in the more general context we are considering.

Theorem 3.5 (Key Theorem).

Let f∈ℳ2⊂k⁡[[X,Y]]f\in\mathcal{M}^{2}\subset k[[X,Y]] be an irreducible Weierstrass polynomial such that S⁡(f)S(f) is tame. Then any family ℱ\mathcal{F} of elements inside k​[[X]]​[Y]k[[X]][Y] of degree in YY less than mult⁡(f){\rm mult}(f) such that

{I⁡(f,h);h∈ℱ}=S⁡(f)∖(S⁡(f)+c⁡(f)−1)\{\operatorname{I}(f,h);\ h\in\mathcal{F}\}=S(f)\setminus\ (S(f)+c(f)-1)

is a representative set of generators of the kk-vector space k⁡[[X,Y]]/J⁡(f)k[[X,Y]]/J(f).

We postpone the proof of this theorem until the next section, since it is long and quite technical.

In order to apply Theorem 3.5 to prove Theorem 3.4 we need a process that transforms a power series into a Weierstrass polynomial. This is classically done by using Weierstrass Preparation Theorem, but this is not appropriate for studying Milnor’s number in positive characteristic, since it involves the multiplication of the power series by a unit and this affects the Milnor number. So, we will need a preparation theorem that involves only coordinate changes and this will be done using a result due to N. Levinson (cf. [Le]) over ℂ\mathbb{C}, which we state so that the same proof remains valid over arbitrary algebraically closed fields.

Levinson’s Preparation Theorem Let 0≠f⁡(X,Y)∈ℳ⊂k⁡[[X,Y]]=k⁡[[X,Y]]0\neq f(X,Y)\in\mathcal{M}\subset k[[X,Y]]=k[[X,Y]], where kk is an algebraically closed field of characteristic p⩾0p\geqslant 0. Write

f=∑i,jαi,j​Xi​Yjf=\sum_{i,j}\alpha_{i,j}X^{i}Y^{j}

where (i,j)∈ℕ2(i,j)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}, and suppose that ff contains for some integer r>1r>1 a monomial YrY^{r} with nonzero coefficient. If rr is minimal with this property and pp does not divide rr, then there exists a change of coordinates φ\varphi in k⁡[[X,Y]]k[[X,Y]], preserving k⁡[[X]]k[[X]], which transforms ff into

φ⁡(f)=A0​(X)​Yr+A1​(X)​Yr−1+⋯+Ar−1​(X)​Y+Ar​(X),\varphi(f)=A_{0}(X)\,Y^{r}+A_{1}(X)\,Y^{r-1}+\cdots+A_{r-1}(X)\,Y+A_{r}(X),

where Ai​(X)∈k​[[X]]A_{i}(X)\in k[[X]] for every ii and

A1​(0)=⋯=Ar−1​(0)=Ar​(0)=0,A0​(0)≠0.A_{1}(0)=\cdots=A_{r-1}(0)=A_{r}(0)=0,\ \ \ A_{0}(0)\neq 0.

For the moment we observe here the following refinement of the above Theorem for the case of plane branches.

Corollary 3.6.

Let f∈k⁡[[X,Y]]f\in k[[X,Y]] be irreducible where kk is algebraically closed of characteristic pp. Set n=mult⁡(f)n={\rm mult}(f). If p∤np\nmid n, then there exists an automorphism φ\varphi of k⁡[[X,Y]]k[[X,Y]] such that

φ⁡(f)=Yn+B1​(X)​Yn−1+⋯+Bn−1​(X)​Y+Bn​(X),\varphi(f)=Y^{n}+B_{1}(X)Y^{n-1}+\cdots+B_{n-1}(X)Y+B_{n}(X),

where Bi​(X)∈k​[[X]]B_{i}(X)\in k[[X]] and mult​(Bi​(X))>i{\rm mult}(B_{i}(X))>i, for all i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n.

Proof: Since ff is irreducible, we have that f=Ln+h​o​tf=L^{n}+hot, where LL is a linear form in XX and YY. By changing coordinates, we may assume that ff is as in the conclusion of Levinson’s Preparation Theorem. Now, since p∤np\nmid n, we take an nn-th root of A0​(X)A_{0}(X) and perform the change of coordinates Y↦Y​A01nY\mapsto YA_{0}^{\frac{1}{n}} and X↦XX\mapsto X. So, after only changes of coordinates φ\varphi, we have that

φ⁡(f)=Yn+B1​(X)​Yn−1+⋯+Bn−1​(X)​Y+Bn​(X),\varphi(f)=Y^{n}+B_{1}(X)Y^{n-1}+\cdots+B_{n-1}(X)Y+B_{n}(X),

is a Weierstrass polynomial, that is, mult​(Bi​(X))>i{\rm mult}(B_{i}(X))>i, for i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n.  

Proof of Theorem 3.4: From Deligne’s results in [De] (see also [MH-W]) and from Lemma 3.1 one always has c⁡(f)⩽μ⁡(f)<∞c(f)\leqslant\mu(f)<\infty.

Now, after a change of coordinates, that does not affect the result, we may assume that the equation ff of CC is a Weierstrass polynomial. For every α∈S⁡(f)∖(S⁡(f)+c⁡(f)−1)\alpha\in S(f)\setminus(S(f)+c(f)-1), take an element g∈k⁡[[X,Y]]g\in k[[X,Y]] such that I⁡(f,g)=α\operatorname{I}(f,g)=\alpha and after dividing it by ff by means of the Weierstrass Division Theorem, we get in this way a family ℱ\mathcal{F} as in Theorem 3.5.

Theorem 3.5 asserts that the residue classes of the elements in ℱ\mathcal{F} generate k⁡[[X,Y]]/J⁡(f)k[[X,Y]]/J(f), hence μ⁡(f)⩽#⁡(S⁡(f)∖(S⁡(f)+c⁡(f)−1))\mu(f)\leqslant\#\left(S(f)\setminus(S(f)+c(f)-1)\right). The result will then follow from the next Lemma that asserts that the number in the right hand side of the inequality is just c⁡(f)c(f).

The μ\mu-stability follows from the fact that for every invertible element uu in k⁡[[X,Y]]k[[X,Y]], both power series ff and u​fuf can be individually prepared into Weierstrass form by means of a change of coordinates that does not alter the semigroup, nor the Milnor numbers. Hence, μ⁡(f)=c⁡(f)=c⁡(u​f)=μ⁡(u​f).\mu(f)=c(f)=c(uf)=\mu(uf).  

Lemma 3.7.

#⁡(S⁡(f)∖(S⁡(f)+c⁡(f)−1))=c⁡(f)\#\left(S(f)\setminus(S(f)+c(f)-1)\right)=c(f).

Proof: In fact, to every i∈{0,1,…,c⁡(f)−1}i\in\{0,1,\ldots,c(f)-1\} we associate si∈S⁡(𝒪)∖(S⁡(𝒪)+c⁡(𝒪)−1)s_{i}\in S(\mathcal{O})\setminus(S(\mathcal{O})+c(\mathcal{O})-1) in the following way:

si={i,if​i∈S⁡(f)i+c⁡(f)−1,if​i∉S⁡(f).s_{i}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}i,&\mbox{if}\ i\in S(f)\\ i+c(f)-1,&\mbox{if}\ i\not\in S(f).\end{array}\right.

The map i↦sii\mapsto s_{i} is injective since S⁡(f)S(f) is a symmetric semigroup. On the other hand, the map is surjective, because, given j∈S⁡(f)∖(S⁡(f)+c⁡(f)−1)j\in S(f)\setminus(S(f)+c(f)-1), we have j=sjj=s_{j} if j⩽c⁡(f)−1j\leqslant c(f)-1; otherwise, if j=i+c⁡(f)−1j=i+c(f)-1 for some i>0i>0, then again by the symmetry of S⁡(f)S(f), it follows that jj does not belong to S⁡(f)S(f) and therefore j=sij=s_{i}.  

We believe that the converse of Theorem 3.4 is true, in the sense that if μ⁡(f)=c⁡(f)\mu(f)=c(f), then S⁡(f)S(f) is a tame semigroup, or, equivalently, if pp divides any of the minimal generators of S⁡(f)S(f), then μ⁡(f)>c⁡(f)\mu(f)>c(f). If this is so, we would conclude from our result that if μ⁡(f)=c⁡(f)\mu(f)=c(f), then CfC_{f} is μ\mu-stable.

To reinforce our conjecture, observe that the result of [GB-P] proves it when mult⁡(f)<p{\rm mult}(f)<p. The following example is a situation where the converse holds and is not covered by the result in [GB-P].

Example 3.8.

Let pp be any prime number and nn and mm two relatively prime natural numbers such that p∤np\nmid n. Then all curves given by f⁡(X,Y)=Yn−Xm​pf(X,Y)=Y^{n}-X^{mp} do not satisfy the condition μ⁡(f)=c⁡(f)\mu(f)=c(f), since μ⁡(f)=∞\mu(f)=\infty and c⁡(f)=(n−1)​(m​p−1)c(f)=(n-1)(mp-1). So, for all p<np<n, we have examples for the converse of our result not covered by [GB-P].

Anyway, the other possible converse of Theorem 3.4, namely, if ff is μ\mu-stable then S⁡(f)S(f) is tame, is not true, as one may see from the following example.

Example 3.9.

Let f=(Y2−X3+X2​Y)2−X11​Y∈k⁡[[X,Y]]f=(Y^{2}-X^{3}+X^{2}Y)^{2}-X^{11}Y\in k[[X,Y]], where char⁡k=5\operatorname{char}{k}=5. Since f3∈ℳ​T​(f)3f^{3}\in\mathcal{M}T(f)^{3} (verified with Singular), then CfC_{f} is μ\mu-stable, but its semigroup of values S⁡(f)=⟨4,6,25⟩S(f)=\langle 4,6,25\rangle is not tame.

Now, to finish the proof of this Lemma we only need to check that h′′h^{\prime\prime} and h′h^{\prime} are indeed the quotient and the remainder, respectively, of the division of hh by fg−1ng−1f_{g-1}^{n_{g}-1}. We will do this by estimating the degree of h′h^{\prime} and, hence, conclude by the uniqueness of the remainder and the quotient in the euclidean algorithm. Indeed, for every summand in h′h^{\prime} we have deg(aJ(X)f0j0⋯fg−1jg−1)<degfg−1ng−1\operatorname{deg}{(a_{J}(X)f_{0}^{j_{0}}\cdots f_{g-1}^{j_{g-1}})}<\operatorname{deg}{f_{g-1}^{n_{g}-1}}, which shows that deg⁡h′<deg⁡fg−1ng−1\operatorname{deg}{h^{\prime}}<\operatorname{deg}{f_{g-1}^{n_{g}-1}}.  

With these tools at hands, we may conclude the proof of Theorem 3.5.

Proof of the Theorem 3.5: Choose ℱ{\mathcal{F}} with minimal number of elements, so from Lemma 3.7 it follows that #​ℱ=c⁡(f)\#{\mathcal{F}}=c(f). In order to do this, it is enough to show that there exists a decomposition k⁡[[X,Y]]=⟨ℱ⟩+J⁡(f),k[[X,Y]]=\langle\mathcal{F}\rangle+J(f), where ⟨ℱ⟩\langle\mathcal{F}\rangle denotes the kk-vector space spanned by the elements of ℱ={φ1,…,φc⁡(f)}\mathcal{F}=\{\varphi_{1},\ldots,\varphi_{c(f)}\}.

The remainder of the division is a YY-polynomial h′h^{\prime} of degree less than v0−1v_{0}-1 and it is sufficient to show that h′h^{\prime} belongs to ⟨ℱ⟩+J⁡(f).\langle\mathcal{F}\rangle+J(f).

If I⁡(f,h′)∈S⁡(f)∖(S⁡(f)+c⁡(f)−1)\operatorname{I}(f,h^{\prime})\in S(f)\setminus(S(f)+c(f)-1) then, according to the definition of ℱ\mathcal{F}, there is an element φis0\varphi_{i_{s_{0}}} such that s0:=I⁡(f,h′)=I⁡(f,φis0)s_{0}:=\operatorname{I}(f,h^{\prime})=\operatorname{I}(f,\varphi_{i_{s_{0}}}). sr=I⁡(f,h′−∑sβs​qs′−∑sαs​φis)∈S​(f)∗+c⁡(f)−1,for all​r⩾N.s_{r}=\operatorname{I}\left(f,h^{\prime}-\sum_{s}\beta_{s}q_{s^{\prime}}-\sum_{s}\alpha_{s}\varphi_{i_{s}}\right)\in S(f)^{*}+c(f)-1,\ \ \ \mbox{for all}\,\,r\geqslant N.

which intersection multiplicity with ff is big enough and which degree is less than deg⁡f\operatorname{deg}{f}. As a final comment, we recall the classical Milnor’s Formula for plane curves singularities that states that if f=f1⋯fr∈ℂ[[X,Y]]f=f_{1}\cdots f_{r}\in\mathbb{C}[[X,Y]] is a possibly many branched and reduced power series over ℂ\mathbb{C} then μ⁡(f)=2​δ​(f)+1−r\mu(f)=2\delta(f)+1-r. A first and natural question after obtaining Theorem 3.4 is:

If all branches f1,…,frf_{1},\ldots,f_{r} have tame semigroups does the preceding formula continues to hold?

We include here some examples to show that this is not always true.

Example 4.5.

Let f=(Y2−X3)2−X11​Yf=(Y^{2}-X^{3})^{2}-X^{11}Y and g=(Y2−X3+X2​Y)2−X11​Yg=(Y^{2}-X^{3}+X^{2}Y)^{2}-X^{11}Y. Then I⁡(f,g)=28\operatorname{I}(f,g)=28 and S⁡(f)=S⁡(g)=⟨4,6,25⟩S(f)=S(g)=\langle 4,6,25\rangle. Here one can compute δ⁡(f​g)=δ⁡(f)+δ⁡(g)+I⁡(f,g)=14+14+28=56.\delta(fg)=\delta(f)+\delta(g)+\operatorname{I}(f,g)=14+14+28=56. Hence 2​δ​(f​g)+1−r=1112\delta(fg)+1-r=111. The behaviour of the reduced 22-branched plane curve singularity defined by the equation f​gfg with respect to μ\mu-stability and the value of e0​(T⁡(f​g))=μ⁡(𝒪f​g)e_{0}(T(fg))=\mu(\mathcal{O}_{fg}) according to the characteristic pp of the ground field is described below. All computations are performed using the software Singular, [DGPS].

(p=7)(p=7) Here (f​g)4∈𝔪​T​(f​g)4(fg)^{4}\in{\mathfrak{m}}\,T(fg)^{4} so that f​gfg is μ\mu-stable. Computation shows that μ⁡(𝒪f​g)=μ⁡(f​g)=112>111\mu(\mathcal{O}_{fg})=\mu(fg)=112>111 so that Milnor’s Formula does not hold. Notice that the semigroups of the branches are tame in characteristic p=7p=7, but p|I⁡(f,g)p\mid\operatorname{I}(f,g).

(p=5)(p=5) Here (f​g)3∈𝔪​T​(f​g)3(fg)^{3}\in{\mathfrak{m}}\,T(fg)^{3} so that again f​gfg is μ\mu-stable. Computation now shows that μ⁡(𝒪f​g)=μ⁡(f​g)=111\mu(\mathcal{O}_{fg})=\mu(fg)=111 and Milnor’s Formula does hold. Notice that the semigroups of the branches are wild in characteristic p=5p=5.

(p=13)(p=13) Here computation shows that μ⁡(f​g)=124\mu(fg)=124 and μ⁡((1+X)​f​g)=114\mu((1+X)fg)=114 so that f​gfg is not μ\mu-stable. Computation also suggests that μ⁡(𝒪f​g)=μ⁡(f​g)=114\mu(\mathcal{O}_{fg})=\mu(fg)=114 and Milnor’s Formula does not hold. Notice that the semigroups of the branches are tame in characteristic p=13p=13 and p∤I⁡(f,g)p\nmid\operatorname{I}(f,g).
